abstract: |
  Tornado detectors trained on radar answer whether a tornado is present now. This project asks
  the question a forecaster needs answered a few minutes earlier: given the scans observed so
  far, will a tornado appear in the next five and ten minutes when none is visible yet? We fine-tune
  the published TorNet detector on that target, evaluate it only on cases where the tornado has
  not yet appeared, and measure it against two fixed references, the detector applied to the
  newest observed scan and the detector applied to the real future scan. On the 2015 slice the
  fine-tuned model edges past the first reference and stays well short of the second. The
  write-up sets out the problem, the data, the experimental setup, the model, and what the
  first results say.
---

# The problem

TorNet [@veillette2024] is a benchmark for tornado detection: storm-centred radar samples with
a label saying whether a tornado is present. The published baseline detector reads one scan and
scores it. That is a detection question, and detection is not what a warning forecaster is
short of in the last minutes before a touchdown. What they need is a signal that arrives before
the signature is unmistakable on the display.

So the question here is a prediction one. Each TorNet sample holds four consecutive scans of a
storm about five minutes apart, each with its own tornado label. We give a model the two oldest
scans and ask it, separately, for the probability of a tornado in each of the two newest: about
five and ten minutes after the last thing the model saw.

The framing has to be protected from detection, because a tornado already on the radar is easy
to carry forward. We therefore score the model only on *pre-onset* cases: tornado samples in
which neither input scan is tornadic and the final target scan is. Samples where a tornado is
already visible in an input scan are reported separately as *ongoing* and excluded from the
positives. Every non-tornadic sample stays in as a negative. The score then answers "will one
appear", not "will one persist".

The negatives come in three flavours, following the TorNet paper: all nulls, random
non-tornadic storms, and storms that were under a tornado warning but produced no tornado. The
last of these is the hard case and the headline number throughout: separating a tornadic storm
from clear air is easy, separating it from a warned storm that looked similar is the job.

Two fixed references turn an AUC into a result. The published detector, frozen, is applied to
the newest observed scan and scored against the future labels: this is the *floor*, the
assumption that the future looks like the present, and it is what a forecaster already has.
The same detector applied to the real future scan is the *ceiling*: what detection would give
if the forecast were perfect. A model lives somewhere between the two, and the result we
report is its paired bootstrap difference from the floor on the same files, with a 95%
interval. The distance from floor to ceiling is the whole prize for forecasting radar, and on
one year it is only 0.05 to 0.07 in AUC.

That smallness, and the rarity of the positives, set the limits of what one year can say.
Pre-onset tornado cases number about 200 to 275 per test year, so any pre-onset AUC carries an
interval of roughly ±0.025, and a difference under about 0.03 is not resolvable. Every comparison
in this project is paired, and seeds and additional years are the only instruments that shrink
the noise.

# The data

TorNet v1.1 is released by MIT Lincoln Laboratory under CC BY 4.0: 203,133 samples from 2013
to 2022, split by the authors into 171,666 training and 31,467 test samples, with 13,857
confirmed tornadoes, 64,510 warned storms and 124,766 random storms. A sample is four NEXRAD
dual-polarisation scans on a polar grid centred on the storm, 120 azimuths by 240 range gates
of 250 m at two elevation tilts, for six products: reflectivity, radial velocity, specific
differential phase, correlation coefficient, differential reflectivity and spectrum width.
Alongside the radar come a range-folding mask for the two Doppler products, the four per-scan
labels, the scan times, the storm's category and EF rating, the tornado's start and end times,
and the chip's azimuth and range limits.

For this project the dataset was repackaged on the Hugging Face Hub as `jakeryderv/tornet`:
every sample and every field as Parquet, 256 samples per shard, the radar stored as half-precision
arrays in physical units with empty gates as NaN. The conversion is lossless and was verified
by reading every shard back completely and comparing random samples with the original files
exactly. A year is one configuration of the dataset, so a training set is a list of years and a
fold is a list of file patterns. The repackaging exists for a practical reason: the original
release is one archive per year, and the experiments need to pick years, partitions and subsets
without extracting and re-reading hundreds of thousands of small files.

The model consumes a scan the way the published detector does. Each product is normalised to
roughly the unit interval with the detector's fixed ranges, empty gates are filled with a
background value of −3, the two range-folding channels are appended to make fourteen channels,
and two coordinate channels, range and its inverse, are derived from the chip's limits for the
detector's CoordConv layers. Keeping this representation is what lets the published weights
serve as the starting point without any adaptation layer.

# Setup

The first slice is 2015: 19,721 training and 3,902 test samples, with 275 pre-onset cases in
the test set. One year is enough to find out whether the approach works at all and cheap
enough to run many variants; the full ten years are the obvious next step and the data layout
makes that a configuration change.

Validation is held out from the training partition by whole days, fifteen percent of them,
never by random sample. Consecutive samples of one storm are near-duplicates, and a random
split would let the validation set see storms the training set had already learned, which
would make early stopping and checkpoint selection meaningless. Checkpoints are selected on
the validation AUC of the model's own output and training stops two epochs after it last
improved.

Loading streams the Parquet shards of the configured years directly from the Hub's file cache,
one shard at a time, reshuffling the shard order every epoch and the rows within each shard.
A shard decompresses to under a gigabyte, so a handful of loader workers hold a handful of
shards and no expanded copy of the dataset is ever written. The published detector's weights
were converted once from the Keras checkpoint to a plain PyTorch state dict, verified to
reproduce the original's logits to within 2×10^-5^ on the 2013 and 2014 test samples, and
published alongside the data, so a fresh checkout needs nothing downloaded by hand.

# The model

The model is the published TorNet detector with as little changed as the question requires.
The encoder is the TorNet CNN: four blocks of CoordConv 3×3 layers with 48, 96, 192 and 384
filters, each block followed by 2×2 max pooling and dropout, ending in a 384-channel map on an
8 × 15 grid of cells. It runs on each of the two input scans with shared weights, initialised
from the published detector and fine-tuned at a tenth of the head's learning rate. The head is
the authors' design as well: two 1×1 convolutions of 512 and 256 channels, a 1×1 convolution to
one logit per cell, and the maximum over the cells, so that the map before the maximum is a
spatial likelihood map of where the model expects the tornado. The whole model has 4.9 million
parameters. The one loss is the weighted binary cross-entropy of each horizon's logit against
the label of the corresponding future scan, with the authors' sample weights, trained with
AdamW, a cosine schedule and mixed precision.

What makes it a prediction model rather than a detector is where time enters, and with two
scans that is a modest place. The two feature maps are concatenated cell by cell, so the head's
first layer sees, for each cell, the features of the older and the newer scan side by side and
can learn any weighted difference between them: a mesocyclone tightening over five minutes, a
reflectivity core moving in. There is no recurrence and no attention; with two steps those
would reduce to the same gated difference at many times the parameters, and earlier
experiments with attention over scans found it tied the concatenation. The temporal reasoning
available is a change detector at the feature level, and that is the honest description of what
two scans allow.

A second combiner makes the time rule explicit instead of learned. With two scans a feature's
history is a line, so each feature can be extrapolated to each horizon as the newest value plus
the per-minute change scaled by that horizon's real lead, read from the scan timestamps rather
than assumed. One shared head, which may start from the published head's weights, then reads
each extrapolated map. The two combiners have the same expressive power; they differ in
inductive bias and in whether the clock is used. An optional consistency term pulls each
extrapolated map toward the encoder's own features of the real future scan, with the target
detached, which asks for a representation whose trend is predictive without drawing any pixels.

An earlier version of the model carried more machinery: a U-Net decoder that drew the future
velocity and reflectivity, trained by a heat-map-weighted L1 and by the frozen detector's
cross-entropy on the drawn chip, meant as an auxiliary signal for the shared encoder. It was
dropped after the comparison reported next.

# Baseline and experiments

All numbers below are on the 2015 test partition, pre-onset cases against warned storms, with
paired bootstrap differences from the floor in brackets.

| horizon | floor | ceiling | with the decoder | encoder + head |
|:--|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| +5 min | 0.709 | 0.764 | 0.716 (+0.007 [−0.030, +0.040]) | **0.739** (+0.030 [−0.006, +0.064]) |
| +10 min | 0.722 | 0.796 | 0.729 (+0.007 [−0.015, +0.031]) | **0.735** (+0.013 [−0.011, +0.038]) |

: Pre-onset WC AUC on 2015, one seed each. {#tbl-baseline}

The decoder did not earn its place. The plain encoder-and-head model matched it at ten minutes
and beat it at five, by +0.023 with an interval of +0.004 to +0.043 on the same files, with half
the parameters and a third less time per epoch. The drawing losses were supposed to lift the
head through the shared encoder; on this year they did not, and the decoder went. Both models
overfit after the second or third epoch on a single year of training data, which is what early
stopping now addresses.

The result that remains is modest and, so far, consistent with every radar-only result in this
line of work. Fine-tuning on the onset target buys about 0.01 to 0.03 over the published
detector applied to the newest scan, with intervals that touch zero, and the ceiling stays
0.055 to 0.074 higher. Two radar scans five minutes apart carry a little of the information
needed to anticipate a tornado ten minutes out, and only a little.

The experiments in progress test that reading and the two design choices made above: the same
model under a second seed, to put a number on the seed noise; the extrapolation combiner with
and without the consistency term; and, next, a gentler encoder learning rate against the
overfitting and a frozen-encoder control that asks whether fine-tuning matters at all. Each is
a fifteen-minute run, and their table replaces this paragraph when they finish.

# What comes next

Two things limit the present numbers, and the data layout now makes both cheap to address.
Training on eight years instead of one attacks the overfitting directly and brings the test set
to a size where differences of a few hundredths become readable. Beyond that, the ceiling says
where the remaining signal is not: even a perfect radar forecast would add at most 0.07, so the
larger gains have to come from information that is not in the radar chip, such as the
near-storm environment, and from longer histories than two scans, where a recurrent combiner
would finally have something to recur over.
